problem: The variance symbols are written flat as σf2 and σe2, so a student reads sigma times f times 2 instead of sigma-squared of the signal and of the error. This is the only formula in the section without the sub/sup tags used elsewhere.
fix: SNR = 10 log<sub>10</sub>(σ<sub>f</sub><sup>2</sup> / σ<sub>e</sub><sup>2</sup>), where σ<sub>f</sub><sup>2</sup> is the variance of the original image and σ<sub>e</sub><sup>2</sup> is the variance of the error.

problem: MAX is squared in the formula but written flat as MAX2, which reads as MAX times 2 and gives the wrong PSNR if a student copies it into an exam.
fix: PSNR = 10 log<sub>10</sub>(MAX<sup>2</sup> / MSE), where MAX is the largest possible pixel value, such as 255 for an 8-bit image.

problem: The reason given, that a code averaging below H would 'leave some symbols indistinguishable', is not the standard argument. The real reason is that no uniquely decodable code can have an average length below H (source coding theorem, via the Kraft inequality); nothing about a short code makes symbols look alike.
fix: H is the average information per symbol. Any code that is uniquely decodable must satisfy Σ 2^(−l_i) ≤ 1, which forces the average code length to be at least H. So no lossless coder can average below H bits per symbol; trying to do so would make some bit strings ambiguous between two different symbol sequences.

problem: Saying 'not R = 75' clashes with the earlier sentence 'R = 0.75, so 75% of the original data was redundant'. Both look like the same statement to a student unless the unit is made explicit.
fix: C = 4 means R = 0.75 as a fraction, that is 75% redundancy. Do not write R = 4, and do not write R = 75 without the percent sign.
